summary: Defines terms used in discussing Internet Fax and describes the goals of the Internet Fax working group, setting a baseline of desired functionality against which proposed protocols can be judged. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Before building a fax-by-internet system, people agreed on the words they would use and what it should do. This document writes that down.

questions: what is a fax onramp and offramp
what are the internet fax operational modes
what is store and forward fax
subtitle: The shared vocabulary and wish list for sending faxes over the Internet, ranked by how badly each feature is wanted.

tldr.problem: Many ways of sending faxes over the Internet had been demonstrated and deployed, and the Internet Fax working group needed common terms and a baseline of goals to judge protocols against.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines roles such as network scanner, network printer, onramp gateway and offramp gateway, three operational modes, and then lists operational and functional goals with priorities {1}, {2} and {3}.
tldr.outcome: It sets requirements rather than a protocol, and any Internet Fax protocol must address its security goals.

today: RFC 2542 is an Informational document that does not specify an Internet standard of any kind, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines goals rather than a protocol.

sections.title: Purpose and Priority Levels
sections.content:
Facsimile has a long tradition as a telephony application for sending a document from one terminal to another. Many mechanisms for sending fax over the Internet had been demonstrated and deployed, and the general application is called Internet Fax. This RFC defines terms and goals to give a baseline against which Internet Fax protocols can be judged, covering 'real-time', 'session' and 'store and forward' delivery.

Desirability is marked with priorities in braces: {1} is a critical characteristic with general agreement, {2} is something most believe is important, and {3} is a useful feature that other factors might override.
sections.eli5: The authors mark each wish as must-have, important or nice-to-have, so everyone knows which ones matter most.

sections.title: Traditional Fax and Internet Fax Roles
sections.content:
'Traditional facsimile' or 'G3Fax' means implementations of T.30 over the telephone network. A user inserts paper, dials, presses start, and the sender negotiates capabilities, scans, compresses and transmits, then is told whether delivery succeeded. This confirmation is an internal signal, not normally visible to the user.

Internet Fax is an application that approximates this user model but uses Internet protocols for some portion of the transmission. The RFC separates four roles that may be combined in any way: a network scanner, a network printer, a fax onramp gateway that takes a fax call and forwards it over the Internet, and a fax offramp gateway that takes an Internet transmission and forwards it to a traditional fax terminal.

These roles can live in many devices: a small 'bump-in-cord' box beside one fax machine, a company PBX onramp, a service bureau, a new Internet fax device, or ordinary Internet hosts with email software. Internet hosts MUST be able to exchange faxes with minimum enhancements, as a {1} goal.
sections.eli5: Old fax machines send pictures of paper down a phone line. Internet Fax does the same but through the Internet, with special doorways (gateways) that connect phone fax machines to the Internet.

sections.title: Store and Forward, Session and Real-Time Modes
sections.content:
The RFC names three modes of Internet Fax. In store and forward, the whole document is stored at a staging point before it moves on, possibly through a series of intermediate agents. In session mode, delivery notification is given to the sending terminal before it disconnects, and direct negotiation and retransmission between the two endpoints are expected.

In real-time mode, two T.30 fax terminals exchange a document so that all the essential elements of the T.30 protocol are preserved, with minimal elongation of the session compared to Group 3 fax on the GSTN. The modes differ in user expectations of immediacy and reliability, in ease of compatibility with legacy terminals, and in the infrastructure they need.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to send. Store and forward is like passing a parcel along a chain of post offices. Session is like a phone call where you hear the answer before you hang up. Real-time is as fast as a normal fax call.

sections.title: Operational Goals
sections.content:
Section 4 lists the traits an Internet Fax protocol needs. It must provide the most commonly used features of traditional fax using only Internet protocols {1}. Interoperability is essential {1}: a compliant sender should not fail because of incompatibility, and this must not depend on the same networking equipment at each end. Interoperability with Internet mail user agents is required {1} only for store-and-forward.

The sender must be able to request notification of delivery and get a determinate answer: delivered, not delivered, or no confirmation possible {1}. Confirmation that a message has been read is desirable {3}, but not required. Other goals are quick delivery on request {2}, a simple minimum feature set with capability exchange so that better devices can work with basic ones {2}, low processing needs {2}, and reliability when capability information is wrong or out of date {2}.

The RFC also says Internet Fax should reconcile fax (immediate delivery, confirmation, ease of use) with email (delayed delivery, no confirmation, replies, many recipients), and should accommodate legal requirements. It quotes United States FCC rules requiring the date and time, the sender's identity and telephone number on the first page or each page.
sections.eli5: The big wishes are that it works between lots of different machines, that you find out whether your fax arrived, and that simple machines and fancy machines can still talk to each other.

sections.title: Functional Goals
sections.content:
Section 5 turns these into goals for specific parts of a protocol. Image formats must be in wide use {1} and able to represent the compression methods of traditional fax {1}, with common MIME mail formats handled {2}. Transmission must work across the Internet, intranets and firewalls {1}.

Addressing must reach every kind of recipient device {1}, including telephone numbers, ISDN modes and fax sub-addresses for offramps. It must allow any email address {1}, with addressing placed only in the email headers and transport envelope. The source of a fax must be clearly identified {1}, and normal email 'reply' should work {2}.

For capabilities, the standard should specify a uniform way to express them {2}, covering sender capabilities, recipient capabilities and the exchange protocol. Capability requests and assertions should identify who they concern and when they apply {2}, and assertions should be protected against interception and substitution.
sections.eli5: These wishes get specific: use a picture format everyone knows, let people be reached by phone number or email address, and let machines tell each other what they can do.

sections.title: Security Goals
sections.content:
The RFC's Security Considerations say that an Internet Fax protocol must address the security goals and provide adequate measures to give users the security features they expect {1}. The goals appear in sections 4.7 and 5.4.

Internet Fax must not cause harm, for example mail loops, bombs, replicated delivery or denial-of-service exposure from automatic notifications and capability exchange {1}. It should not release private information by default {2}. Users expect fax to be confidential and unaltered, so Internet Fax should give privacy and integrity as good as or better than telephone-based fax {2}. Minimum-capability devices should still accept signed messages, even if they ignore the signature {2}. Authentication and secure billing information for offramp services are desirable {3}.
sections.eli5: Sending faxes over the Internet should be at least as private as a phone call, and should never create new ways to annoy or harm people.

items.label: Critical
items.desc: General agreement that this is a critical characteristic of any definition of Internet Fax.

items.label: Important
items.desc: Most believe this is an important characteristic of Internet Fax.

items.label: Useful
items.desc: A useful feature, but other factors might override; omitting it is acceptable.

items.title: Network scanner
items.text: Scans a paper document and sends the image via the Internet.

items.title: Network printer
items.text: Accepts an image sent via the Internet and prints it automatically.

items.title: Fax onramp gateway
items.text: Accepts a facsimile telephone call and forwards it via the Internet.

items.title: Fax offramp gateway
items.text: Accepts a transmission from the Internet and forwards it to a traditional fax terminal.
